blocks.text: Dear Ms. Hall:

You asked us to find out whether the assumptions behind the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} retirement plan still describe your workforce. We are glad to do that work. This letter sets out what the study will cover, how we will carry it out, who will do it, and the terms under which we will both work. We have tried to keep it plain. If a question about the engagement comes up later, this letter is where we will both look first.
What the study will cover

Every valuation of the plan rests on assumptions about people: when they retire, how many leave before they retire, how many become disabled, how long retirees live, and how quickly pay rises. An experience study sets those assumptions beside what actually happened to the plan's members over a recent period of years. Where the two differ, and we judge the difference likely to last, we will recommend a change.

The study will examine rates of retirement, termination of employment, disability, and death, and the rate of salary increase. We will settle the study period with you once we have seen which years of data are available. It needs to be long enough to give stable results and recent enough to reflect the plan as it operates now.

Some work falls outside this letter. We will not value the plan, review the investment return or inflation assumptions, or advise on plan design. If you would like any of that, we will propose it separately.
How we will reach our recommendations

We will keep two kinds of work apart from start to finish. The first is measurement. We count what happened in the data and compare it with what the current assumptions expected to happen. Anyone with the same data could repeat that part and get the same answer. The second is judgment. We decide whether a difference is large enough, and steady enough, to justify a new assumption. One unusual year can move the counts a long way. When that happens we will say so, and we will not let that year set an assumption on its own.

The report will follow the same division. For each assumption it will show the observed experience, the rate we recommend, and our reasons. Where a recommendation rests more on judgment than on the data, the report will say that in so many words.

We will perform the work under the Actuarial Standards of Practice. Those that bear most directly on it are No. 23, Data Quality; No. 35, on demographic and other noneconomic assumptions for pension obligations; and No. 27, on economic assumptions, which governs the salary scale. Our report will also meet No. 41, Actuarial Communications.
The data we will rely on

Our results can be no better than the records behind them. We will rely on data and documents supplied by {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. We will review them for consistency and reasonableness, and we will tell you what we find, but we will not audit them. To begin, we will need the following:

items: 1. Participant census files for each year of the study period, covering active employees, former employees with deferred benefits, retirees, disabled members, and beneficiaries.
2. For each person who left active employment during the period, the date of departure and the reason, as your records show it.
3. Pay history for active employees over the same years.
4. The plan document, and any amendment adopted during the period that changed when members could retire or what they would receive.
5. The most recent actuarial valuation report, including its description of the current assumptions.

blocks.text: Please send the files in whatever form your systems already produce. Nobody on your staff should spend time reformatting them for us.
The team

I will lead the engagement and sign the report. David Sherman, Senior Analyst, will load the census files, link each member's records from one year to the next, and reconcile them to the valuation data. Jeffrey Ochoa, Actuarial Analyst, will build the experience tables and the comparisons of actual and expected results. Megan Dudley, Actuarial Associate, will work with your staff on the data request, on missing records, and on any question about a file.
Day to day, you will hear most from Megan and David. If you have a concern about the work at any point, please raise it with me.
Start date and fee

We will begin work on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}. We expect the study to take about four months from that date. How quickly the data arrive, and how many questions they raise, will decide most of that schedule.

Our fee for the study described in this letter is {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}}. The fee is fixed. It covers the data work, the analysis, a draft report, a meeting with you to go through the draft, and the final report.
Fees and payment

We will invoice the fee in installments: one when work begins, one when we deliver the draft report, and one when we deliver the final report. Invoices are payable within thirty days of receipt. If you ask us for work outside this letter, we will confirm it with you in writing first and bill it at our standard hourly rates.
Term and termination

This engagement runs from the start date above until we deliver the final report and answer your questions on it. Either of us may end it sooner by written notice to the other. If that happens, you will pay for the work done up to the date of the notice, and we will return or destroy your data as you direct.
Confidentiality

The census files will contain personal information about your employees, former employees, and their families. We will hold that information in confidence, keep it on secure systems, and use it only for this study. We will not disclose it outside our firm without your written consent unless the law requires us to.

Our report will be prepared for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} and for the plan. You may give it to the plan's auditors and to any agency that oversees the plan. No one else may rely on it without our written consent.
Limitation of liability

We will carry out the work with the care and skill expected of a qualified actuary. We are not responsible for errors that come from data or information supplied to us. Our total liability for any claim arising from this engagement will not exceed the fees you have paid us under this letter.
Governing law
The laws of the state in which our principal office is located govern this letter. If a court finds any part of it unenforceable, the remaining terms still apply.
If this letter matches your understanding of the engagement, please sign below and return a copy to me. Once it is back, Megan Dudley will contact your office to arrange the first transfer of data.
Very truly yours,
Memorandum

To: Robert Lawrence, Jeffrey Ochoa, Megan Dudley
From: David Sherman, Senior Analyst
Subject: Experience study for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}, opening plan

The study is set up and waiting on data; the census files are the only item holding up the first counts. Work began on {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}. Our objective is a set of recommended assumptions for the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} retirement plan, covering retirement, termination, disability, mortality, and salary increase, each supported by the plan's own experience as far as the data allow and by a stated judgment where they do not. Barbara Hall, Chief Operating Officer, is our client contact. Requests to the company go through her office, and any change to scope needs her agreement before we act on it.

One rule applies to every item below. Each table will carry the observed rate and the recommended rate in separate columns, and the two are not interchangeable. The observed rate is a measurement and should be reproducible by anyone holding the same files. The recommended rate is a judgment. Its reason belongs in the working file at the time the judgment is made, in a sentence Robert can review and, if he accepts it, carry into the report.
How the work is divided

items: 1. Data intake and linking: David Sherman. Load each year's census as received, link members across years, and classify every change in status. Each year's closing count must equal the following year's opening count, or the difference must be explained in the data log.

2. Client questions on data: Megan Dudley. Megan is the single contact for the client's staff on files, missing records, and corrections. Questions go out in batches, and each one states what we will assume if no answer comes back.

3. Decrement tables: Jeffrey Ochoa. Build exposures and actual decrements by age and service for retirement, termination, disability, and death, and compute expected decrements under the current assumptions. The table layouts are to be agreed with Robert before any data run through them.

4. Salary experience: Jeffrey Ochoa, with David Sherman. Measure pay increases by service for members active in consecutive years. Exclude any record where a pay change coincides with a change in status, and log the exclusions.
5. Recommendations and report: Robert Lawrence. Robert reviews each recommended assumption against its table and its stated reason, settles any open question of judgment, and signs the report.

Before the files arrive

items: 1. Megan Dudley sends the data request to Barbara Hall this week. It repeats the file list from the engagement letter and attaches our preferred layout as a suggestion only; files in the company's own format are acceptable.

2. David Sherman sets up the study files and the data log, and enters the current assumptions from the most recent valuation report so that expected decrements can be computed as soon as data are loaded.
3. Jeffrey Ochoa drafts the table shells and proposed age and service bands for Robert's review.
4. Robert Lawrence confirms the assumptions in scope against the engagement letter and sets the study period once we know which years of data the company can supply.

blocks.text: We will meet weekly while the data are open. I will circulate the data log before each meeting.
Good morning Barbara,

The census files for the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} study are loaded, and every file links cleanly to the one before it except the most recent. That file needs your help before we count any terminations or retirements.

A large share of the employees active in the prior year's file do not appear in the most recent file under the same employee number. Most of them are there under new numbers, with the same names, dates of birth, and hire dates. Taken at face value, the files would show each of them leaving and a new employee being hired in their place. That would overstate turnover and distort the termination rates. We have not adjusted anything yet.
To resolve it, we would need the following:

items: 1. Confirmation of whether employee numbers were reissued in the past year, for example in a change of payroll or HR system.
2. If they were, any crosswalk your staff hold from the old numbers to the new ones.
3. If no crosswalk exists, your agreement that we match records on name, date of birth, and hire date instead.

blocks.text: So that the work does not stall, we will run a provisional match on those three fields this week and treat it as preliminary until we hear from you. A few smaller record questions will come separately from Megan; none of them holds up the study.

Best,
David
Good morning Barbara,

I would like to add one question to David's while your staff look into the employee numbers. The files tell us what happened. They cannot tell us on their own whether a year was ordinary. If a group of employees left at once, we need to know why before we let that year shape the termination or retirement rates.
It would help us to know:

items: 1. Whether {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} had any layoffs or reductions in force during the study period.
2. Whether you offered an early retirement window or any other incentive to leave.
3. Whether any location or business unit was sold or closed.

blocks.text: None of this will change the counts. It will change how much weight we give them, and our report will say which years we treated differently and why. A short answer is fine for now. We can follow up on any item that needs more detail.

Sincerely,
Robert
Good morning Barbara,

The provisional match has closed most of the gap. Matching on name, date of birth, and hire date pairs nearly all of the unmatched records from the prior year's {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} file with records in the most recent file under new numbers.

What remains is a smaller group who were active in the prior file and do not appear in the most recent one under any number. On the data alone, these look like genuine departures within a single year. They are the people Robert's questions bear on, and we will hold the termination tables until we know whether something lay behind them. This result is preliminary and will be rerun if a crosswalk turns up.
To finish this step, we would need:

items: 1. Your agreement for us to send the list of these records to your HR staff through our secure file transfer site, so they can check each one against their files.
2. The reason recorded for each departure, where your HR system holds one.

blocks.text:
Best,
David
Good morning Barbara,
David's match is good news for the study. The question is now much narrower. It concerns one group of people who left in one year, and nothing else in the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} files.

We will not treat that year as unusual unless your records give us a reason to. If it turns out to be ordinary turnover, it stays in the counts like any other year. If there was an event behind it, we will measure it, show it separately in the report, and base the termination assumption on the remaining years.
To keep the work moving this week, we need:

items: 1. A short answer to the questions in my earlier note, even if only for the most recent year.
2. The name of someone on your HR staff whom Megan can work with on the record-level check.

blocks.text:
Sincerely,
Robert
